unmapped_findings: The high stacking fault energy of the low density steel (80–110 mJ/m²) makes the austenite-to-martensite (TRIP) transformation theoretically impossible, motivating the study of deformation-induced ferrite↔austenite transformations. [b0013]

Thermo-Calc predicts three phases for the Fe-11.15Mn-5.6Al-0.07C system: (1) BCC_A2 (ferrite), (2) FCC_A1 (austenite) and (3) BCC_A1#2, a BCC-structured phase with an extremely high Mn content; Mn partitions preferentially to austenite and Al to ferrite. [b0027]

After deformation at 500 °C at 0.001 s⁻¹ to true strain 0.6, SEM composition analysis (Table 1) showed Mn enriched in austenite (12.8 ± 0.1 wt% vs 10.3 ± 0.1 wt% in ferrite) and Al enriched in ferrite (6.0 ± 0.1 wt% vs 4.7 ± 0.1 wt% in austenite). [b0035, figure_unlabelled_002]

Simultaneous deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) and deformation-induced austenite transformation (DIAT) occurred along the deformation bands at 500 °C, releasing shear-strain localization; these transformations were not observed in the microstructure deformed at the higher temperature of 600 °C. [b0023]

Slip in the ferrite is accommodated by activation of multiple slip systems {110}<111> and {112}<111>, producing intersecting slip bands and wavy dislocation movement that promotes dislocation-cell formation and high dislocation density walls (HDDWs). [b0022]

The parent austenite was effectively sheared through propagation of the deformation bands, and the bidirectional ferrite↔austenite transformation was justified thermodynamically by the exactly equal Gibbs energy of ferrite and austenite resulting from Al/Mn elemental partitioning (Mn partitioning mainly dictates phase stability). [b0028, b0036]
